prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping lets many neutral atoms be interrogated without first-order light-shift error, and for its development to a fractional uncertainty of about 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B047 with Katori and Ye as my preferred single-part prize, after testing it again against the first-round exchange and the chair's questions. The distinctness argument, which is the real crux, can be put in one sentence: the frequency comb (2005) supplies the means to count optical cycles and Wineland's ion control (2012) supplies a single, well-isolated absorber, but neither offers a way to hold thousands of neutral atoms tightly enough to remove Doppler and recoil effects while cancelling the first-order light shift of the trapping field, and Katori's magic-wavelength condition is exactly that. This matters scientifically and not only as a matter of labelling. A single ion gives a clock whose statistical uncertainty is bound to long averaging times, whereas a lattice of many atoms makes it possible to resolve and evaluate systematic shifts at the 10^-18 level within hours; that is what allowed Ye's group and others to compare clocks across laboratories and to approach centimetre-scale gravitational redshift sensitivity. The result is also reproduced and surpassed by several independent groups, so maturity is not in question. On credit, Katori's proposal and Ye's demonstration of the strontium instrument is the cleanest two-name attribution on the shortlist; nobody has questioned that the supplied pair is right, only whether others should be added. I do not rest this on the redefinition of the second, which I regard as a consequence and not a precondition of the prize.
statement.case_against: I have to weigh the objections in the same terms I apply to B006, as the chair asks. First, B006 has clearly broader reach and far wider opening support, with seven of eight members placing it in their top three, and I accept that a topological prize touches more communities than a metrology prize does. Second, the 2005 and 2012 prizes do cover the enabling toolkit, and a committee reading the lattice clock as a refinement of precision spectroscopy could reasonably conclude that the increment is too small; I think that reading understates the magic-wavelength principle, but I cannot make the question disappear and the non-atomic members have said they cannot test it independently. Third, the ion-clock groups, and other early lattice-clock contributors such as the proposers and first demonstrators in other laboratories, are outside the credited names, and my recollection of the precedence sequence is from memory. Finally, my own field proximity and my research stay in Hall's laboratory create a real risk that I overweight this case, so I am treating the six-member B006 majority as information about breadth and not as something to be dismissed.

responses.point: Respects B047 and finds its attribution the cleanest on the shortlist, but regards B006 as broader in reach, since it changed what a whole community measures and calculates, and asks whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay the clock case.
responses.response: On the redefinition: no, I would not delay for it. The prize criterion is the invention and its demonstrated consequences, and clock-to-clock comparisons at the 10^-18 level already establish those. A metrology-body decision is an administrative follow-on, and waiting for it would have the prize trail the metrologists rather than recognise the physics. On reach I concede your point rather than argue it away: B006 serves more communities, and I do not claim equal breadth. What I contest is whether breadth should decide between two mature, well-defined discoveries when the cost of the broader one is a visible omission of Hasan and of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang. A narrower prize with a complete credit is not obviously the weaker prize, and the clock has reach of its own into tests of constants and geodesy.

responses.point: Agrees that B047 is clean and keeps it as first alternative, but says the step from the 2005 and 2012 prizes to lattice clocks must be argued as a distinct invention and finds the discovery content of topological insulators broader.
responses.response: I take the chair's challenge as the right one and have tried to answer it in one sentence in my case: combs count the cycles, ion control provides the absorber, and the magic-wavelength lattice is what lets a large neutral ensemble be used at all without first-order light-shift error. I also hold B006 to the same standard, and I notice that your own case against it, the cost of dropping Hasan or Mele and the overlap with 2016, is about as large as my case against B047. If those costs are judged smaller than the novelty concern, the committee will reasonably prefer B006, and I would not call that a scientific error. I do not agree that discovery content is the deciding measure, since the statutes also name invention, and the lattice clock is an invention with a quantified, replicated result.

responses.point: Agrees with the ranking and the two names, but warns that shared atomic-physics background must not do the work of an argument, and notes the ion-clock community as a legitimate adjacent claim.
responses.response: I agree, and the committee should hold both of us to that. The difference between us seems to be small: you keep B006 as first alternative partly because attribution there is unresolved, while I add a view on timing. I would add one thing to your point on ion clocks. Their strongest claim is for precision, not for the many-atom principle, so I would handle it in the citation by naming the lattice and magic-wavelength trapping rather than adding names; I have written my citation that way. If you or any non-atomic member can see a way in which that wording still overreaches, I would want to hear it, since neither of us is placed to be the sole judge of our own neighbourhood.

responses.point: Argues topological insulators are the strongest case and the clearest discovery in the statutory sense, with two decades of independent confirmation, while the attribution cost (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Hasan under a three-person cap) is the real weakness.
responses.response: I agree with your account of the maturity of B006 and I do not dispute the science; the HgTe observation is decisive and two decades of ARPES, transport and STM make the interpretation stable. We differ on how heavily to count the attribution weakness you yourself identify: your own uncertainty list says that whichever trio is chosen leaves out someone with a substantial claim, and that is a cost B047 does not carry. For the chair's question about B006 citation wording, I would suggest the narrowest version, naming the Z2 classification, the quantum spin Hall state and its observation in HgTe wells, and saying nothing about three-dimensional materials, since otherwise the citation implies a recognition the trio cannot support. I do not think Hasan should replace Mele; that judgement lies in condensed-matter physics and I defer to those members.

responses.point: Ranks B006 first as the strongest combination of conceptual originality, experimental confirmation and breadth, notes that the three names match the theory-plus-experiment structure, and sees the 2016 overlap as answered by the 2D and 3D Z2 step being distinct.
responses.response: Your reading of the 2016 distinction, time-reversal symmetry and spin-orbit coupling in a band insulator versus 1D chains and quantum Hall topology, is persuasive to me as a non-specialist, and it is the main reason I would not oppose B006 on scientific grounds. Where I would press is the claim that breadth makes it the safer prize: a prize with an acknowledged contested credit boundary between the 2D and 3D stories is exposed in a way a two-name clock prize is not. I take the point that six of eight members have moved to the same trio, but the chair notes some of those moves followed colleagues' arguments, so I read that as partly convergent and weigh it less than the number suggests.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the earlier recognised comb and ion-control prizes; non-atomic members say they cannot judge this, so the question may not be fully resolved by discussion.
Precedence among early lattice-clock proposals and demonstrations, and whether ion-clock or other lattice groups should be credited, is from memory and was not verified.
How the committee should weigh B006's much broader support and reach against its unresolved attribution and the 2016 overlap, compared with B047's narrower reach and clean attribution.
My own lineage and field affinity may lead me to overrate B047, so I treat the six-member B006 majority as informative about breadth.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: my doctoral period included a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall is closely tied to the precision-spectroscopy and frequency-comb lineage to which Jun Ye's work belongs; no direct collaboration with Katori or Ye is documented in my profile, but I may have a scientific-lineage affinity for B047, and as an atomic physicist I may be assessing my own neighbourhood. Separately, my Lund quantum-information and quantum-memory work and my WACQT role relate to B031 and B038, which I name only as an alternative (B031) and which would call for a recusal discussion if either became the preferred prize. I have no documented connection to B006 or its credited names.
